lines: Build HitCounter() with hit(t) (record a hit at second t) and getHits(t) (hits in the past 300 seconds, i.e. with timestamps in (t − 300, t]). Timestamps never decrease.

a1.cap: For example, with the calls HitCounter(), hit(1), hit(2), hit(3), getHits(4), hit(300), getHits(300), getHits(301), the answer is [null,null,null,null,3,null,4,3].

lines: Input: the calls HitCounter(), hit(1), hit(2), hit(3), getHits(4), hit(300), getHits(300), getHits(301)

a1.cap: Hits arrive in time order, so keep their timestamps in a queue. Before answering, drop timestamps that slid out of the 300-second window from the front; the queue length is the answer.
Let's walk through it with the calls HitCounter(), hit(1), hit(2), hit(3), getHits(4), hit(300), getHits(300), getHits(301).
a1.say: Let's walk through it with the calls Hit Counter, hit(1), hit(2), hit(3), get Hits(4), hit(300), get Hits(300), get Hits(301).

a1.cap: 3 hits in the last five minutes.
4 hits in the last five minutes.
A hit is older than 300 seconds at time 301, so drop it.
3 hits in the last five minutes.
Time complexity is O(1) amortised and extra space is O(window).
a1.say: Time complexity is O of one amortised and extra space is O of window.

a1.cap: That's the Sliding Window Queue approach. Now try writing it yourself, in Java or Python!
